Sadness
SAD-nes
n. (sorrow of countenance; which Ecclesiastes says makes the heart better)
From Old English saed, sated or weary. At Ecclesiastes 7:3 it renders Hebrew roa panim, literally badness of face — a face gone heavy.

Biblical Definition

Ecclesiastes states a thing nobody wants to hear and states it flatly: Sorrow is better than laughter: for by the sadness of the countenance the heart is made better. The Hebrew is literally the badness of the face — a countenance gone heavy — and the verse claims that a heavy face does something to a heart that a light one does not. The surrounding verses press the point: It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to go to the house of feasting: for that is the end of all men; and the living will lay it to his heart, and The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning; but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth.

The claim is not that gloom is godly. Ecclesiastes elsewhere commends bread eaten with joy and a garment always white. The claim is that a funeral tells the truth about the human situation and a party does not, and that a man who has stood at a graveside and laid it to his heart is in a better position to live than a man who has arranged never to go. Paul sharpens the distinction the New Testament makes on the whole subject: godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death. Two sorrows, and they look identical from outside. One drives a man to God, and the other drives him further in on himself.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): sorrowfulness; mournfulness; dejection of mind; gravity of countenance.

expand to see more

SADNESS, n. Sorrowfulness; mournfulness; dejection of mind; also, seriousness; gravity.

SAD, a. Sorrowful; affected with grief; cast down; also, serious; grave; not gay or volatile.

MOURNING, n. The act of sorrowing or expressing grief; lamentation; the dress or customary habit worn by mourners.

COUNTENANCE, n. The whole form of the face; the system of features; the face; aspect; look.

GRAVE, a. Of weighty character; serious; sober; solemn; not light, trifling or jocose.

Key Scripture

Ecclesiastes 7:3 — "Sorrow is better than laughter: for by the sadness of the countenance the heart is made better."

Ecclesiastes 7:2 — "It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to go to the house of feasting: for that is the end of all men; and the living will lay it to his heart."

2 Corinthians 7:10 — "For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death."

Nehemiah 2:2 — "Wherefore the king said unto me, Why is thy countenance sad, seeing thou art not sick? this is nothing else but sorrow of heart. Then I was very sore afraid,"

Modern Corruption

Sadness is treated as a malfunction to be eliminated, and a church shaped by that assumption has nothing to say at a graveside and nothing to do with Ecclesiastes 7.

expand to see more

The prevailing assumption is that sorrow is a problem, and the only question is which method removes it. Ecclesiastes says something no modern discourse will say: that sorrow is better than laughter, and that a heavy face improves a heart. The Bible is not romanticizing misery; it is observing that grief teaches what comfort cannot, that the house of mourning tells the truth about the end of all men, and that the wise deliberately go there. A congregation that has made its gatherings a permanent house of mirth has made itself useless to its own members on the worst day of their lives.

At the same time Scripture refuses to bless all sorrow indiscriminately. Paul's distinction is exact and is the one thing a grieving believer most needs: godly sorrow works repentance, and the sorrow of the world works death. Judas and Peter both wept. One went out and hanged himself and the other was restored by a charcoal fire on a beach. The difference was not the depth of the grief but its direction. Anyone working through his own sadness has one useful question — does this drive me toward God or away from Him? — and Scripture treats the answer as decisive.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew roa panim (H7455 / H6440), badness of face; ebel (H60), mourning; Greek lupe (G3077), grief.

expand to see more

Hebrew roa (H7455) — badness, sadness; joined to panim, the face, for a countenance gone heavy.

Hebrew ebel (H60) — mourning; the house of mourning in Ecclesiastes 7:2.

Hebrew kaas (H3708) — vexation, grief; the sorrow better than laughter.

Greek lupe (G3077) — grief, sorrow; the noun Paul divides into two kinds.

Greek metanoia (G3341) — repentance; what the godly kind works.

Usage

"“by the sadness of the countenance the heart is made better” — a claim nobody wants."

"“The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning” — where the wise choose to be."

"“godly sorrow worketh repentance... the sorrow of the world worketh death” — direction, not depth."
